content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with planners, presenters, and content experts, have disclosed that neither they nor their spouses or partners have any financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. The planners have reviewed the content to ensure it is free from bias. The content does not include discussions of unlabeled uses of products or investigational uses of products, except where recommendations may differ from package labeling. Antibiotic resistance is one of the most significant public health threats today, causing an estimated 2 million infections and 23,000 deaths annually in the United States. Antibiotics are life-saving drugs essential to modern medicine, but infections caused by pathogens resistant to first-line antibiotics often require alternative treatments that are more expensive and potentially toxic. These resistant infections increase healthcare costs and, more importantly, lead to higher morbidity and mortality rates. The primary modifiable risk factor for antibiotic resistance is the inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics. Approximately half of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions in humans may be inappropriate, including errors in antibiotic selection, dosing, or duration, as well as unnecessary prescriptions. At least 30% of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions in the United States are unnecessary. Antibiotic stewardship refers to efforts to measure and improve antibiotic prescribing and usage by clinicians and patients. This includes ensuring antibiotics are prescribed only when necessary, minimizing misdiagnoses or delayed diagnoses that lead to underuse, and selecting the correct drug, dose, and duration when antibiotics are required. Antibiotic stewardship can be implemented in all healthcare settings where antibiotics are prescribed and is a cornerstone of improving patient safety and slowing the spread of antibiotic resistance. The goal is to maximize the benefits of antibiotic treatment while minimizing harm to individuals and communities. Improving antibiotic prescribing in all healthcare settings is critical to combating antibiotic-resistant bacteria. In developed countries, 80-90% of antibiotic use occurs in outpatient settings. In the United States in 2013, approximately 269 million antibiotic prescriptions were dispensed from outpatient pharmacies. About 20% of pediatric visits and 10% of adult visits in outpatient settings result in an antibiotic prescription. Complications from antibiotics range from common side effects like rashes and diarrhea to severe allergic reactions. Adverse drug events from antibiotics lead to an estimated 143,000 emergency department visits annually and contribute to excess healthcare resource use. Antibiotic treatment is the most important risk factor for Clostridium difficile infection (CDI). In 2011, an estimated 453,000 cases of CDI occurred in patients without recent overnight stays in healthcare facilities. Up to 35% of adult and 70% of pediatric CDI cases are community-associated. A 10% reduction in overall outpatient antibiotic prescribing could reduce community-associated CDI cases by 17%. Reducing unnecessary antibiotic prescribing through stewardship can prevent avoidable adverse events. In 2014 and 2015, the CDC released the Core Elements of Hospital Antibiotic Stewardship Programs and the Core Elements of Antibiotic Stewardship for Nursing Homes. The 2016 report, Core Elements of Outpatient Antibiotic Stewardship, provides guidance for improving outpatient antibiotic prescribing and use. It is intended for outpatient healthcare professionals and leaders in primary care, specialty clinics, emergency departments, retail health, urgent care, dentistry, and community pharmacies, as well as healthcare systems involved in outpatient care. Leaders of organizations of any size and specialty are encouraged to commit to optimizing antibiotic prescribing and patient safety. They should implement at least one policy or practice to improve prescribing, track and report antibiotic prescribing practices, educate clinicians and patients on appropriate use, and ensure access to expertise on antibiotic prescribing. Before implementing stewardship interventions, clinicians and outpatient clinic leaders should identify high-priority conditions for intervention, barriers to improving prescribing, and standards for appropriate antibiotic use. High-priority conditions include those where clinicians commonly deviate from best practices, such as overprescribing, underprescribing, or misprescribing antibiotics. Barriers may include knowledge gaps, perceived patient expectations, time pressures, or concerns about patient satisfaction. Standards for prescribing should be based on national clinical practice guidelines or facility-specific guidelines. Antibiotic stewardship interventions should be evidence-based and tailored to the outpatient setting. Clinicians can use delayed prescribing practices or watchful waiting when appropriate, provide communication skills training, and require written justification for non-recommended antibiotic prescriptions. Tracking and reporting antibiotic prescribing practices, also known as audit and feedback, can guide practice changes and assess progress. Individualized feedback to clinicians is an effective way to promote adherence to evidence-based guidelines. The CDC developed the Core Elements of Outpatient Antibiotic Stewardship by consolidating evidence-based practices and adapting best practices from other clinical settings. A narrative review of evidence on outpatient stewardship interventions was conducted, including systematic reviews and expert opinions. Subject-matter experts provided feedback on the feasibility, acceptability, and potential impact of the core elements. The Core Elements of Outpatient Antibiotic Stewardship include commitment, action for policy and practice, tracking and reporting, and education and expertise. Commitment involves demonstrating dedication to optimizing antibiotic prescribing and patient safety. Actions for policy and practice include implementing evidence-based diagnostic criteria and treatment recommendations. Tracking and reporting involve monitoring prescribing practices and providing feedback to clinicians. Education and expertise ensure access to resources and knowledge for optimizing antibiotic use. Outpatient clinicians and healthcare leaders are encouraged to use checklists to assess and implement stewardship activities. These checklists can help identify opportunities for improvement and guide interventions to enhance antibiotic prescribing practices.
